newsitem.title: EGYPT: FEATURE - Palestinian air flies into turbulent horizon.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Palestinian air flies into turbulent horizon.

text.p: It took the approval of a king and a long bus ride across the desert before Palestinians cleared the obstacles of Middle East politics and launched their new airline's first international flights this month.
"There was applause on take-off and landing," said Palestinian Airlines Chairman Fayez Zaidan of the inaugural flight PV-141. "We said PV stands for Palestinian Victory."

After agreement with Egypt and personal approval from Saudi Arabia's King Fahd, the "national" carrier of the Palestinian Authority (PA) flew more than 300 Gazan pilgrims on seven charter flights from Port Said to Jeddah.

In what may be the world's longest trip from ticketing to tarmac, the Palestinians took a bus from Gaza across the Sinai and to northern Egypt in a trip of more than 13 hours because Israel would not let the planes fly from Gaza airport.
The charter flight series, which ended this week, reflected the turbulence of Middle East politics more than it did the start of an emerging commercial venture.

But Zaidan said he hoped the deal under which Israel turned over 80 percent of Hebron in the occupied West Bank to Palestinian self-rule would make way for plans for privatisation, purchase and lease deals and scheduled flights.
"I think things will go on once the Hebron problem is solved," Zaidan said before the deal was concluded.

"Normally these flights should take off from Gaza," said Zaidan about the territory that Israel in 1993 turned over to Palestinian self-rule under Oslo peace accords. "But we have started our flights to declare the start-up of the airline."
AIRPORT ON PEACE TALKS AGENDA
Under the accord it concluded with the Palestinians in mid-January to redeploy troops from Hebron, talks will start between Israel and the Palestinians on opening Gaza airport.

Israel agreed to allow construction of Gaza airport under the Oslo accord but the Jewish state, which has overall security control of the territories it has occupied since 1967, has demanded the airport fall under its auspices.
The airline must operate "in exile" in Egypt until Israel agrees in a special protocol to let it fly from the Gaza airport.
"I hope within two to three months from now we will sign the protocol regarding the operation of Gaza International Airport and then we will start up our regular flights," Zaidan said.

Zaidan said the airline plans its first international regular flights from Gaza to Cairo, Larnaca and Amman. He is working on accords to fly to Tunisia, Mauritania, Greece, Italy, Turkey and Britain and Gulf states including Saudi Arabia.

It was because of the lack of a bilateral air transport agreement with Saudi Arabia that Palestinian President Yasser Arafat personally had to ask King Fahd to let the pilgrimage planes land, Zaidan said.
But he added there were also political implications.
"Because we were Palestinian Airlines, nobody could give the green light politically except his majesty the king," he said.
The flights marked the first time that the PA's airline visited foreign airports.
ISRAEL HESITATES
Zaidan, who is involved in the protocol talks, said the Palestinians have offered air traffic and security liaison offices to the Israelis to allay their security concerns.
But he also saw Israeli hesitation in letting the airline and airport operate because of what he said were the implications for Palestinian statehood.

"The main problem for the Israeli side is not the security. But I believe the main problem is the airport and the airline are among the most important symbols of the Palestinian sovereignty and statehood," Zaidan said.
After the airline -- with the red, green, black and white stripes of the Palestinian flag -- starts to fly from Gaza, Zaidan hopes for a six month teething period before they invite investors.

"As one of the decision makers of this airline, it will be to some extent 50-50," he said of the targeted equity share. "I prefer also to have Palestinians as shareholders but the matter of having foreigners in the airline may be discussed."
He said there were talks under way to lease one of the airline's two Fokker 50s this month to keep it operating.

Zaidan said the airline's assets of $35 million included equipment and the planes, and that it had 30 percent losses from the $200,000 it cost the airline to make the pilgrim flights. He said they had to pay Saudi Arabia a $52 royalty per passenger.
"Anyhow in our case we do not consider that this is a loss," Zaidan said. "This is a declaration, and I believe we gained politically more than we lost."
